Announced after an international consultation, the recommendations reflect the continuing evolution of influenza viruses and the need to update vaccines regularly. Seasonal flu causes substantial illness and many hospitalizations each year, making a close match between vaccine composition and the viruses expected to circulate an important part of protection against severe illness and death. The World Health Organization has recommended the virus strains to include in influenza vaccines for the Southern Hemisphere's 2027 flu season, giving manufacturers and national regulators the guidance needed to prepare for another year of seasonal infections. Announced after an international consultation, the recommendations reflect the continuing evolution of influenza viruses and the need to update vaccines regularly. Seasonal flu causes substantial illness and many hospitalizations each year, making a close match between vaccine composition and the viruses expected to circulate an important part of protection against severe illness and death. Tracking changing viruses to prepare for the next season Experts from WHO Collaborating Centres and Essential Regulatory Laboratories meet twice a year to review global surveillance findings and recommend vaccine compositions for upcoming influenza seasons. Their assessments draw on the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and other sources, helping national vaccine regulatory agencies and pharmaceutical companies develop, produce and license vaccines. This process connects information gathered by laboratories across the world with decisions about the vaccines that will become available for the following season. Surveillance from February to August 2026 found influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses circulating in varying proportions across every region. Influenza A viruses were the most common in most regions, with influenza B dominating in Northern and Western Africa, North America and Eastern Asia. These geographical differences form part of the evidence experts review when assessing which viruses upcoming vaccines should cover, with recommendations reflecting the broader picture of influenza activity. The recommended strains depend on how vaccines are made For egg-based vaccines, WHO recommends three components: an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus, an A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus, and a B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus. This combination covers the two influenza A subtypes and the influenza B lineage specified in the recommendation, giving manufacturers using egg-based production a defined composition for vaccines intended for the 2027 southern hemisphere season. For vaccines made using cell culture, recombinant protein or nucleic acid technologies, the recommended components are an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus, an A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like virus, and a B/Pennsylvania/14/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus. The H1N1 recommendation is shared across both groups, with different named H3N2 and B/Victoria components specified for these production methods. The precise strain designations provide the technical guidance needed to develop and assess vaccines for the coming season. Animal influenza remains part of pandemic preparedness The consultation examined influenza viruses circulating in animals, particularly those that have infected people, because these zoonotic viruses remain a significant concern for their potential to cause pandemics. WHO's twice-yearly meetings include detailed assessments of these threats and the selection of new candidate vaccine viruses from contemporary zoonotic influenza viruses. These candidates can support rapid vaccine manufacturing if a pandemic threat emerges, with information on newly selected candidates available through WHO's published recommendations. Dr Maria Van Kerhove, WHO's Director for Epidemic and Pandemic Management, credited nearly 75 years of GISRS work with demonstrating the value of international cooperation in public health. Countries and laboratories sharing data, viruses and expertise make timely vaccine recommendations possible and strengthen the ability to detect and respond to emerging influenza threats. That cooperation underpins both the routine work of preparing seasonal flu vaccines and the continuing effort to keep vaccine options ready for viruses that could pose a wider danger. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu WHO selects viruses for 2027 southern hemisphere flu shots News brief September 25, 2026 Chris Dall, MA Topics Influenza Vaccines Share quantic69 / iStock The World Health Organization (WHO) today announced the composition of flu shots for the 2027 influenza season in the southern hemisphere. The composition of the vaccines is decided by a group of experts the WHO convenes twice a year in February and September. At these meetings, the group reviews data on circulating flu viruses generated through the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and makes recommendations for upcoming flu seasons in the northern and southern hemispheres. Flu season in the southern hemisphere typically stretches from April through September but can last until October or November. In the September meeting, experts reviewed flu activity from February through August, which was dominated by influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and influenza B viruses. For egg-based vaccines, the WHO recommends the following: an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus; an A/Darwin1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus; and a B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus Recommendations for cell culture-, recombinant protein-, or nucleic acid-based vaccines include: an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus; an A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like virus; and a B/Pennsylvania/14/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus. The group also reviews flu viruses circulating in animals to monitor for potential pandemic threats. ‘Global public health collaboration at its best’ The WHO’s director for epidemic and pandemic management said GISRS demonstrates “the power of global solidarity in public health.” "The commitment of countries and laboratories to share data, viruses and expertise enables WHO to make timely vaccine recommendations, strengthening our collective ability to detect and respond to emerging influenza threats,” Maria Van Kerkhove, PhD, said in a news release. “This is global public health collaboration at its best." US measles cases continue to climb, topping 3,600 News brief September 25, 2026 Chris Dall, MA Topics Measles wildpixel / iStock The US measles count has climbed to 3,659 confirmed cases, with 171 new cases added this week, according to today’s update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Of the 3,659 confirmed cases, 18% are in children age 5 and under, 43% in children and teens aged 5 to 19, and 38% are in adults 20 and older. Nine percent of case-patients have been hospitalized. Ninety-five percent of case-patients are unvaccinated or have unknown vaccination status. The CDC also now lists one measles death for the year, though Pennsylvania has reported four measles-associated deaths. The agency says it’s working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized definition of deaths due to measles. The one death has an asterisk next to it. “This number is subject to change; CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed,” the CDC said. There have now been 40 new measles outbreaks reported so far this year (one new); 95% of all confirmed cases are linked to outbreaks that started this year or in 2025. An outbreak is defined as three or more cases. A total of 5,948 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the United States since the beginning of 2025. In 2024, there were 285 confirmed cases. 129 more cases in Pennsylvania Pennsylvania remains the nation’s hot spot, with 129 new cases in the past seven days and 890 for the year, according to an update today from the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Lancaster County, where two of the state’s measles deaths have been reported, has been the hardest hit, with 342 cases. Other states with notable increases in measles cases include Ohio, which added nine new cases this week and now has 189 for the year; Kentucky, which added 10 new cases and has 67 for the year; and Wisconsin, which added four new cases and has 171. Ebola cases, deaths in DR Congo outbreak near 7,900 and 3,800 as virus spreads to 2 more health zones News brief September 25, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Ebola United Nations Photo / Flickr cc As the Ebola virus spreads to two new health zones in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and cases and deaths mount, G20+ leaders have pledged $2.9 billion to help fight the outbreak. Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) said the Bundibugyo Ebola virus has infiltrated two more health zones, Bulu in Sud Ubangi and Dunghu in Haut Uele province, raising the total number of affected health zones to 63 in seven provinces. Case and death numbers have reached 7,890 and 3,799, respectively, for a crude case-fatality rate (CFR) of 48.1%. “At the national level, the number of new cases reported each day remains high,” the WHO said. “However, the situation varies across the country, with some provinces and health zones experiencing much higher levels of transmission than others.” “The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care,” the agency added. ‘Pledges alone will not stop Ebola’ The financial commitments, announced at the G20+ Foreign Ministers Meeting on Accelerating Collective Action to Defeat Ebola in New York this week, consist of cash and in-kind assistance, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said in a press release yesterday. The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care. “We thank the US for this leadership and sense of solidarity by convening the 20 Ministerial meeting,” Jean Kaseya, MD, MPH, Africa CDC director general, said in the release. “But pledges alone will not stop Ebola. We must be able to trace every single dollar—from commitment to disbursement, from implementing partner to expenditure, and ultimately to the services delivered to affected communities.” At the meeting, the United States pledged an additional $267 million in health and humanitarian assistance for the outbreak, for a total of $887 million. “With this new life-saving global health assistance, the United States will directly scale up support to combat the outbreak through new Ebola treatment units, additional safe and dignified burial teams, mass procurements of personal protective equipment, expanded surveillance, critical health commodities, and contact tracing through trusted implementers,” the Department of State said in a news release. Quick takes: NWS-related border reopening, dengue in Florida, NIH PubMed tool, sprout recall, more polio News brief September 25, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics New World Screwworm Dengue Foodborne Disease Polio E coli The Santa Teresa livestock crossing in New Mexico reopened yesterday, 18 months after it closed to contain the importation of New World screwworm (NWS) from Mexican cattle, per media reports. In announcing the reopening, US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins noted that the pest has not been eradicated from the United States and that the crossing will stay open only if Mexican authorities continue to meet the terms of a joint surveillance and treatment plan. So far this year, NWS has been detected in 49 animals in Texas and New Mexico, including a recent case in a horses in Texas and New Mexico. Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas counties in west-central Florida have declared states of emergency to battle dengue fever amid rising cases of the mosquito-borne disease, including one death, in Hillsborough. A Hillsborough emergency order is meant to allow the county to take certain actions to control the mosquito population and pursue federal reimbursement of some expenses. As of September 23, 177 dengue cases had been confirmed in the county. While case counts are low in Pasco and Pinellas counties (two and seven, respectively), the emergency will allow officials to work to prevent the disease from further spreading across county lines, WUSF reported. The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) yesterday launched a new artificial intelligence–informed PubMed tool designed to boost the replication and reproducibility of NIH-funded research. The tool, Linked Discoveries, allows scientists to more easily visualize how an individual research finding relates to the larger body of biomedical evidence. So far, the tool links to more than 29 million PubMed publications. This week, Berlin Seeds recalled alfalfa sprout seed after one person became ill and the seed supplier notified the company that the finished sprouts were part of a US Food and Drug Administration investigation of a multistate foodborne illness outbreak caused by Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli and Salmonella Agona. A spent irrigation water sample from one seed lot also tested positive for E coli. The seeds were sold at the company’s store in Millersburg, Ohio, and online from February 13 to August 26 to customers in 44 states. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative this week reported seven cases of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) in Afghanistan with paralysis onsets in August, one case of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) in Chad with a paralysis onset in July, and three cVDPV2 cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with paralysis onsets in June and August. Afghanistan now has 32 WPV1 cases in 2026, compared with 21 last year. The composition of the vaccines is decided by a group of experts the WHO convenes twice a year in February and September. At these meetings, the group reviews data on circulating flu viruses generated through the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and makes recommendations for upcoming flu seasons in the northern and southern hemispheres. Flu season in the southern hemisphere typically stretches from April through September but can last until October or November. In the September meeting, experts reviewed flu activity from February through August, which was dominated by influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and influenza B viruses. For egg-based vaccines, the WHO recommends the following: an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus; an A/Darwin1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus; and a B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus Recommendations for cell culture-, recombinant protein-, or nucleic acid-based vaccines include: an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus; an A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like virus; and a B/Pennsylvania/14/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus. The group also reviews flu viruses circulating in animals to monitor for potential pandemic threats. ‘Global public health collaboration at its best’ The WHO’s director for epidemic and pandemic management said GISRS demonstrates “the power of global solidarity in public health.” "The commitment of countries and laboratories to share data, viruses and expertise enables WHO to make timely vaccine recommendations, strengthening our collective ability to detect and respond to emerging influenza threats,” Maria Van Kerkhove, PhD, said in a news release. “This is global public health collaboration at its best." US measles cases continue to climb, topping 3,600 News brief Chris Dall, MA Topics Measles wildpixel / iStock The US measles count has climbed to 3,659 confirmed cases, with 171 new cases added this week, according to today’s update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Of the 3,659 confirmed cases, 18% are in children age 5 and under, 43% in children and teens aged 5 to 19, and 38% are in adults 20 and older. Nine percent of case-patients have been hospitalized. Ninety-five percent of case-patients are unvaccinated or have unknown vaccination status. The CDC also now lists one measles death for the year, though Pennsylvania has reported four measles-associated deaths. The agency says it’s working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized definition of deaths due to measles. The one death has an asterisk next to it. “This number is subject to change; CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed,” the CDC said. There have now been 40 new measles outbreaks reported so far this year (one new); 95% of all confirmed cases are linked to outbreaks that started this year or in 2025. An outbreak is defined as three or more cases. A total of 5,948 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the United States since the beginning of 2025. In 2024, there were 285 confirmed cases. 129 more cases in Pennsylvania Pennsylvania remains the nation’s hot spot, with 129 new cases in the past seven days and 890 for the year, according to an update today from the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Lancaster County, where two of the state’s measles deaths have been reported, has been the hardest hit, with 342 cases. Other states with notable increases in measles cases include Ohio, which added nine new cases this week and now has 189 for the year; Kentucky, which added 10 new cases and has 67 for the year; and Wisconsin, which added four new cases and has 171. Ebola cases, deaths in DR Congo outbreak near 7,900 and 3,800 as virus spreads to 2 more health zones News brief Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Ebola United Nations Photo / Flickr cc As the Ebola virus spreads to two new health zones in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and cases and deaths mount, G20+ leaders have pledged $2.9 billion to help fight the outbreak. Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) said the Bundibugyo Ebola virus has infiltrated two more health zones, Bulu in Sud Ubangi and Dunghu in Haut Uele province, raising the total number of affected health zones to 63 in seven provinces. Case and death numbers have reached 7,890 and 3,799, respectively, for a crude case-fatality rate (CFR) of 48.1%. “At the national level, the number of new cases reported each day remains high,” the WHO said. “However, the situation varies across the country, with some provinces and health zones experiencing much higher levels of transmission than others.” “The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care,” the agency added. ‘Pledges alone will not stop Ebola’ The financial commitments, announced at the G20+ Foreign Ministers Meeting on Accelerating Collective Action to Defeat Ebola in New York this week, consist of cash and in-kind assistance, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said in a press release yesterday. The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care. “We thank the US for this leadership and sense of solidarity by convening the 20 Ministerial meeting,” Jean Kaseya, MD, MPH, Africa CDC director general, said in the release. “But pledges alone will not stop Ebola. We must be able to trace every single dollar—from commitment to disbursement, from implementing partner to expenditure, and ultimately to the services delivered to affected communities.” At the meeting, the United States pledged an additional $267 million in health and humanitarian assistance for the outbreak, for a total of $887 million. “With this new life-saving global health assistance, the United States will directly scale up support to combat the outbreak through new Ebola treatment units, additional safe and dignified burial teams, mass procurements of personal protective equipment, expanded surveillance, critical health commodities, and contact tracing through trusted implementers,” the Department of State said in a news release. Quick takes: NWS-related border reopening, dengue in Florida, NIH PubMed tool, sprout recall, more polio News brief Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics New World Screwworm Dengue Foodborne Disease Polio E coli The Santa Teresa livestock crossing in New Mexico reopened yesterday, 18 months after it closed to contain the importation of New World screwworm (NWS) from Mexican cattle, per media reports. In announcing the reopening, US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins noted that the pest has not been eradicated from the United States and that the crossing will stay open only if Mexican authorities continue to meet the terms of a joint surveillance and treatment plan. So far this year, NWS has been detected in 49 animals in Texas and New Mexico, including a recent case in a horses in Texas and New Mexico. Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas counties in west-central Florida have declared states of emergency to battle dengue fever amid rising cases of the mosquito-borne disease, including one death, in Hillsborough. A Hillsborough emergency order is meant to allow the county to take certain actions to control the mosquito population and pursue federal reimbursement of some expenses. As of September 23, 177 dengue cases had been confirmed in the county. While case counts are low in Pasco and Pinellas counties (two and seven, respectively), the emergency will allow officials to work to prevent the disease from further spreading across county lines, WUSF reported. The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) yesterday launched a new artificial intelligence–informed PubMed tool designed to boost the replication and reproducibility of NIH-funded research. The tool, Linked Discoveries, allows scientists to more easily visualize how an individual research finding relates to the larger body of biomedical evidence. So far, the tool links to more than 29 million PubMed publications. This week, Berlin Seeds recalled alfalfa sprout seed after one person became ill and the seed supplier notified the company that the finished sprouts were part of a US Food and Drug Administration investigation of a multistate foodborne illness outbreak caused by Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli and Salmonella Agona. A spent irrigation water sample from one seed lot also tested positive for E coli. The seeds were sold at the company’s store in Millersburg, Ohio, and online from February 13 to August 26 to customers in 44 states. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative this week reported seven cases of wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) in Afghanistan with paralysis onsets in August, one case of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) in Chad with a paralysis onset in July, and three cVDPV2 cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with paralysis onsets in June and August. Afghanistan now has 32 WPV1 cases in 2026, compared with 21 last year. content: Home National Influenza Positivity Rate Hits 56% in Indonesia: What to Know Translator Bardjan Editor Bardjan Senin, 28 September 2026 19:19 WIB A health worker administers a swab test on a patient during an early detection test for super flu at the Serpong 1 Community Health Center, South Tangerang, Banten, January 7, 2026. Medically, super flu is triggered by coinfection, or infection with multiple viruses at once, such as a combination of Influenza A and COVID-19 variants. This condition is exacerbated by a decline in the population's natural immunity (immunity debt) following the easing of global health protocols. Antara/Muhammad Iqbal TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Indonesia’s Health Ministry recorded an influenza positivity rate of 56 percent in the 38th week of 2026, but said the figure remains within the medium range and does not yet indicate a concerning situation. Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin said in Jakarta on Monday that the increase in influenza cases should be addressed by strengthening surveillance and preparedness rather than triggering panic. Influenza Activity Remains in Medium Range Budi said influenza activity detected through surveillance at community health centers, known as puskesmas, has reached the medium category, while surveillance at hospitals remains in the low category. “There has indeed been an increase in influenza cases, particularly in Indonesia and Southeast Asia. But based on the surveillance data we have, the situation remains within the medium range. Therefore, what we are doing is strengthening surveillance and preparedness so that developments in cases can continue to be monitored,” Budi said, as quoted by Antara. According to Health Ministry data, the increase in influenza activity in August and September remains consistent with the seasonal pattern typically observed in Indonesia. In the 38th week of 2026, 148 of 265 specimens tested through sentinel surveillance were positive for influenza. Influenza A (H1N1pdm09) was the dominant strain. What the Data Says About ‘Superflu’ The Health Ministry is also monitoring the spread of Influenza A (H3N2) subclade K, which has recently drawn public attention and has been referred to as “superflu.” The term “superflu” is not an official nomenclature used by the World Health Organization (WHO) or the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to refer to subclade K. The ministry therefore said influenza developments should be assessed based on test results and surveillance data rather than solely on terminology circulating among the public. Budi said surveillance data showed that detections of subclade K this year were lower than last year. “For what is being referred to as ‘superflu’ or H3N2 subclade K, the data we are monitoring actually show that the number of detections this year is lower than last year. So, we need to distinguish between information circulating among the public and conditions reflected in surveillance data,” Budi said. Based on ILI-SARI sentinel surveillance, 188 subclade K detections were recorded from 2025 through the 38th week of 2026. Of these, 166 were recorded in 2025 and 22 in 2026. The Health Ministry continues to monitor subclade K through sentinel surveillance involving puskesmas, hospitals, and laboratories and health quarantine centers. Who Needs Antiviral Treatment? According to Antara, Budi said most influenza cases can recover with supportive care and do not require hospitalization. Antiviral drugs such as oseltamivir are not intended for every influenza patient. “Oseltamivir must be used appropriately. Based on input from experts, the drug should be used selectively for patients with severe conditions or those with comorbidities who require antiviral treatment,” Budi said. Restricting oseltamivir use is necessary to prevent antiviral resistance, he said, comparing the risk to inappropriate antibiotic use, which can contribute to antimicrobial resistance. “We must not overuse antivirals because there is a risk of resistance. If resistance develops, we could lose treatment options when facing a more severe and life-threatening outbreak, such as H5Nx influenza,” he added. Health Ministry Urges Vigilance, Not Panic The Health Ministry is continuing to strengthen influenza surveillance, healthcare facility preparedness, laboratory capacity, and risk communication with the public. The ministry urged people to remain vigilant by maintaining good hygiene, wearing masks when sick or in crowded places, practicing proper cough and sneeze etiquette, and seeking medical attention if symptoms worsen. Vulnerable groups, including infants and young children, older adults, pregnant women, and people with underlying health conditions, require greater attention because they face a higher risk of complications. “Recognize the symptoms, prevent transmission, and seek medical attention promptly if the condition worsens,” Budi said. The recommendations are based on global influenza surveillance data collected through the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and other sources. WHO updates influenza vaccine composition twice a year because circulating influenza viruses continually evolve, requiring vaccines to be adjusted to maintain protection against the strains expected to cause disease. From February to August 2026, influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and influenza B viruses circulated across regions worldwide. Influenza A viruses were predominant in most regions, while influenza B viruses dominated in Northern and Western Africa, North America, and Eastern Asia. Upcoming Conferences and Events Physical EventOct 1st, 2026 Beat 2026: 2nd Edition of National Cardiovascular Summit & Awards 2026 For the 2027 Southern Hemisphere season, WHO has recommended vaccine compositions targeting A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage viruses. The specific recommended strains vary depending on whether vaccines are produced using egg-based or cell culture-, recombinant protein-, or nucleic acid-based technologies. WHO also assessed influenza viruses circulating in animals, particularly zoonotic viruses that have infected humans. These viruses remain an important area of pandemic preparedness because of their potential to develop into viruses capable of sustained human transmission. The biannual review also supports the selection of candidate vaccine viruses (CVVs) from contemporary zoonotic influenza viruses, which could help accelerate vaccine development and production if a pandemic influenza threat emerges. (Massoud Hossaini | TribLive) At the University of Pittsburgh’s Vaccination and Health Hub in Oakland, students are already preparing for the cold and flu season. “We vaccinate students, faculty, staff and the general community,” said Kate Brownlee, executive director of the Hub. What started in 2020 as a site meant to administer the covid-19 vaccine has grown into a center where students can better protect themselves against respiratory illnesses. Located on Fifth Avenue, the Hub is participating in the first Pennsylvania College and University Flu Challenge, which the Pennsylvania Department of Health launched in anticipation of this year’s cold and flu season, Brownlee said. The Hub received its first shipment of the flu vaccine at the beginning of the month, and its student clinicians have started administering doses to their classmates. As fall begins, Brownlee and other health experts are echoing the advice of state and local officials. “Get vaccinated,” Brownlee said. But when is the right time to get a flu shot? Where should people go, and is it free? How severe could this flu season be, and what should someone do if they get sick? How bad will flu season be Neil Ruhland, a spokesman for the Pennsylvania Department of Health, said predicting the severity of flu season is challenging. “Because seasonal influenza is driven by viral mutations and changing personal habits, predicting the exact course of any flu season is difficult,” Ruhland said. Dr. Brian Lamb, an internal medicine doctor at Allegheny Health Network, said it is too early to tell how severe the flu season will be this year. “We don’t have the signs yet,” Lamb said. “What we worry about is last year we saw very dismal rates for vaccination, and we worry that we’re going to see the same poor rates of vaccinations.” Cases of influenza virus are up since this time last year from 204 cases in the 2024-25 season to 303 cases in the 2025-26 season, according to data from the Pennsylvania Department of Health. The Allegheny County Health Department said it has confirmed 147,640 cases of influenza since last September, while data from mid-September 2026 showed 22,010 adult and 4,108 pediatric hospitalizations since this time last year. There have been 545 flu-related deaths reported in Pennsylvania for the 2025-26 season. “We expect that influenza A (H1N1), influenza A (H3N2), and influenza B/Victoria lineage will be circulating over the next few months,” Ruhland said. “The exact dominant flu strain cannot be predicted with certainty before the season develops.” Last year, the new flu variant subclade K swept across the United States and raised concerns about the effectiveness of the flu vaccine. Ruhland said “influenza viruses continually mutate throughout a respiratory virus season,” but he did not say they could anticipate what new mutations will come this season. Allegheny County Health Department Medical Director Jillian Irwin said a particularly bad flu season in Australia last year should serve as a reminder to get an updated vaccine as strains of influenza evolve. “This year’s flu vaccine has been updated because the virus has changed,” Irwin said. “We should prepare ourselves in advance rather than wait for friends and family members to start getting sick.” Although flu variants remain the same, Lamb said, they experience what is called a “genetic drift” when they circulate from person to person. “Every time it goes into the human body, it mixes around and then you cough it up and it changes just a little bit,” Lamb said. “Imagine it like trying to make soup and everyone keeps coming into the kitchen and adding spices.” Symptoms, treatment and prevention Symptoms of the flu, according to Lamb, are very similar to other respiratory illnesses. If someone is not vaccinated, symptoms can be more severe. “More severe cough, fever, muscle aches, breathing difficulties,” Lamb said. “Also, you could expect a longer course. If you’ve had the shot and develop the flu, you may have symptoms for fewer days.” The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the flu can develop without symptoms, but common signs of illness include fever or feeling feverish/chills, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headaches and fatigue. Some people may have vomiting and diarrhea, though this is more common in children than adults. Ruhland anticipates symptoms for flu season will not change this year. Featured Local Businesses We Buy Property LLC 905 Bingham St , Pittsburgh, PA, 15203 Diversity Moving Company 3948 Monroeville Blvd Ste 6, Monroeville, PA, 15146 Movers More local businesses Lamb said flu testing kits are available at pharmacies, and recommended self-testing or scheduling a doctor’s appointment if symptoms develop. He also recommended over the counter medicines Robitussin, Advil, Tylenol, Flonase and Tamiflu. “Usually, you want to start Tamiflu within 48 hours of developing the symptoms,” Lamb said. “Biggest thing I’d recommend is making sure you have the chance to rest.” Lamb said if symptoms last for several days or hinder daily activities, people should be evaluated by a medical professional. The state health department affirmed that getting vaccinated annually “remains the single most effective way for Pennsylvanians to protect themselves from severe illness, hospitalization and death.” Brownlee said that, as childhood vaccination rates decline, the Hub’s mission is to support those who want to protect themselves against illness. “Our goal is not to push vaccines on anyone,” Brownlee said. “It’s to answer people’s questions and make sure that people feel supported and cared for in whatever way that we can.” While the statewide university vaccination effort yields no reward for the institutions involved, Brownlee said the goal is to keep people healthy. “We’re just going to try to do the best we can to get as many people vaccinated as we can,” Brownlee said. Brownlee recommended frequent hand-washing in the coming weeks and staying at home whenever possible if symptoms develop. She also recommended wearing masks at your discretion to prevent contracting or spreading the virus. Getting vaccinated Irwin said everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine unless advised otherwise by their doctor. To give the body time to build immunity before the height of flu season, Lamb and Irwin advise patients to get vaccinated between September and October. “It takes about two weeks to get coverage from your flu shot,” Lamb said. “That two weeks is when your body is really starting to make antibodies ... starting to get your defenses primed for you so that you’re ready coming into the winter season.” Irwin added that getting vaccinated after that window closes is still “worthwhile.” However, Lamb warned against getting the shot too early, as immunity becomes less effective over time. “An updated flu vaccine is now available across the commonwealth,” Ruhland said. Ruhland added that the updated vaccines were recommended by the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, including the three primary flu strains (H1N1, H3N2, and B/Victoria). The primary strains of the flu are determined by prior circulation of the influenza virus around the globe, and “what is expected to be circulating in the coming months,” Ruhland said. Irwin said standard flu shots, a nasal spray for many people ages 2 through 49, and egg-free vaccines will be available this season. “The best of these options is generally the one that is appropriate for your age and health and that you can receive on time,” Irwin said. Adults 65 and older should ask about a high-dose or “extra-strength” flu shot, which can produce a larger immune response, Irwin added. Brownlee recommended talking to primary care physicians and local pharmacists to find out which vaccine will be most effective. Lamb said the mFLUSIVA vaccine, which was approved by the FDA this year for adults 50 and older, should present no problems for patients. “They’re safe. They’re effective,” Lamb said. Between Monday and Friday at the Hub, anyone can make an appointment or walk in to the clinic for their flu shot, which is covered under most regional insurance plans. The center is open until 7 p.m. Monday through Thursday. If the shot is not covered, Brownlee said, patients are referred to a clinic where the shot can be administered. At CVS, the shot is also covered by most insurance plans, but if patients pay out of pocket or through a third party, prices vary: $99 for a standard-dose flu shot and $144 for either a senior-dose shot or Flublok — a higher antigen, egg-free flu vaccine. Irwin said the Allegheny County Health Department is also offering immunizations at the Pittsburgh clinic on First Avenue by appointment or walk-in. Featured Local Businesses We Buy Property LLC 905 Bingham St , Pittsburgh, PA, 15203 Diversity Moving Company 3948 Monroeville Blvd Ste 6, Monroeville, PA, 15146 Movers More local businesses The department accepts most insurance plans, while out-of-pocket costs range from $32 to $76, depending on the type of vaccine administered. Lamb said while no vaccine is “100 percent effective,” getting vaccinated ahead of flu season can dramatically reduce the severity of flu symptoms if the illness is contracted

More info Thank you for subscribing A pharmacist is urging people to check whether they can get a free flu jab as medics brace for an influx of K-strain super-flu this winter. Concerns over a particularly nasty winter flu season in the UK come as doctors in New Zealand battle a major outbreak of the disease. Subclade K is a genetic offshoot of Influenza A(H3N2). It spreads rapidly because it features subtle genetic mutations that allow it to transmit efficiently through populations. Because of these drift mutations, older flu vaccine formulations show reduced protection against infection from subclade K. H3N2 strains tend to hit older adults and vulnerable groups harder than H1N1 or Influenza B strains. The severity seen with subclade K is a feature of H3N2. READ MORE: Strictly week 1 leaderboard in full as fans fume contestant was 'done dirty' READ MORE: Illness-ravaged Exeter Chiefs 'quite poor' in heavy defeat by Gloucester New Zealand public health professor Michael Baker fears his country faces an “historically” high death rate this flu season, pointing to a sharp rise in people being sent to hospital. There has been a late surge in the flu season in New Zealand, and Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) has issued warnings regarding sharp upticks in community sickness and primary care visits. The late-winter surge prompted health officials to encourage the public to use urgent care clinics and telehealth options to ease pressure on emergency departments. The outbreak is piling pressure on hospitals, with under-fives recording higher rates of influenza-related hospitalisation and severe illness than any other age group. The fast-spreading flu bug - which can trigger chills, fever and headaches - has prompted New Zealand health authorities to expand their free flu jab programme to children aged six months to under five.. Experts in Britain routinely watch the southern-hemisphere winter for clues about what could lie ahead during the UK's own flu season. This year, influenza A/H3 has been the predominant strain identified by experts, with all sequenced samples belonging to subclade K. For the 2025–2026 winter season, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) estimated 3,798 influenza-attributable excess deaths in England. Deputy Superintendent at Well Pharmacy, Wendy Lee, is urging people to get protected before winter sets in - but in particular is calling on anyone eligible to get their free vaccination. She said: “The crisis in New Zealand should be a wake-up call to us all - particularly parents of young children, the old and vulnerable. CONTINUE READING “Flu can come on very quickly, so now is the time to think about protection rather than waiting until cases are already rising. Don’t be fooled into thinking that the winter is going to be any less harsh because of the enduring heatwaves during this long summer.” Who can get a free flu jab? The NHS 2026/27 flu vaccination programme is already getting under way. Since September 1, two and three-year-olds, primary school children and secondary school children have been eligible for a free NHS flu jab, in England and Wales. Pregnant women have also been eligible for vaccination since September 1, while most other eligible groups are due to start from October 1. These include: Adults aged 65 and over People aged 18 to 64 in clinical risk groups Pregnant women Children born between 1 September 2022 to 31 August 2024, or that are in school from Reception through to Year 11 People living in long-stay residential care homes Carers Other groups specified under the national flu vaccination programme.[6] Wendy said : “If you're eligible for a free NHS jab, you should check how and where you can get vaccinated, rather than waiting for flu levels to rise.” Well Pharmacy's free NHS flu vaccination service begins from October 1, in England and Wales, subject to eligibility and availability. Private flu vaccinations are available now at Well Pharmacy. For people who are not eligible for a free NHS jab, Well Pharmacy's private flu vaccination service is currently listed at £19.49. Information on eligibility, tips on managing symptoms and staying healthy is available on the Well Pharmacy flu vaccination page. Is it flu or a cold? How to tell... Wendy said: “Flu can be confused with a bad cold because some of the symptoms overlap. But one of the biggest differences is how quickly symptoms appear.” According to the NHS, flu symptoms can come on very quickly and can include: a high temperature a dry cough aching body tiredness headache sore throat a runny or blocked nose chills loss of appetite Some people can also experience nausea or diarrhoea.[9] Flu is highly contagious and can affect the nose, throat and lungs. Show more Wendy said: “There are tests that can detect influenza A or B from a nose/throat sample. Some rapid tests give results within minutes, while molecular tests are more accurate. “Routine testing isn't usually needed for otherwise healthy people though, because you and/or medical professionals can often diagnose flu from your pattern of symptoms.” What is the ‘K’ strain - and how do I know if I have it? Wendy said: “The ‘K’ strain is a subclade of influenza A/H3, and its symptoms are not known to be distinct from those of other seasonal flu. Taking a test can confirm whether you have influenza or if it's just a cold, but identifying the specific K subclade requires more specialised laboratory analysis.” Although advocating for all those eligible to get their flu jabs, Wendy cautions against being overly panicked. She said: “The evidence so far suggests K is not necessarily more severe than other flu strains in an individual person. The reason it is causing such a big impact appears to be how easily it is spreading and the sheer number of people being infected. “Populations have built up immunity to flu strains that have circulated in recent seasons, but K has evolved significantly from these viruses, meaning there is likely to be less natural immunity to it. This may be contributing to its high transmissibility, making vaccination an important way for eligible people to reduce their risk of becoming seriously unwell and help protect those around them.” Will Britain get the same outbreak? There is no guarantee the UK is facing the same outbreak as New Zealand - nor whether the same K-strain will reach our shores. Last year, concerns around a so-called ‘Aussie flu’ grew following an especially bad season in Australia. While the UK saw an earlier-than-usual spike in infections in mid-October, cases of the virus peaked in December and declined through January and February. Despite the grave concerns of health experts, the 2025/2026 winter flu season led to 3,798 deaths - less than half than the 9,740 deaths recorded during the 2024/2025 season. Show more Nevertheless, New Zealand’s high level of influenza activity and hospital does provide a valuable early-warning for Britain as it heads into winter. For those who qualify for a free NHS flu jab, the message from health experts is simple: check your eligibility and don't leave it too late waiting til the flu virus is already spreading widely. Wendy said: “Remember, it takes about two weeks after a flu vaccination for your body to develop antibodies and reach its expected level of protection. The NHS warns the flu vaccine usually takes up to 14 days to work. “This means you are not protected, you can still catch flu during those first two weeks if you're exposed before your immune response has developed.” Follow Devon Live FacebookTwitter Comment

content: News Sports Autos Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH How long does flu shot last? What experts say this fall Jenna Prestininzi USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Sept. 25, 2026, 9:51 a.m. ET Hear this story The arrival of fall in Michigan means the peak of flu season is not far away, and experts say getting vaccinated now will give you protection throughout the season. The flu shot provides lifesaving protection against severe illness and prevents spreading the flu to your loved ones, according to the American Lung Association. Experts recommend getting your flu shot by late October, and even in September if possible, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Once you're vaccinated, it'll take about two weeks for antibodies offering protection against the illness to develop in your body, the CDC says. The vaccination will protect you throughout flu season. Immunity declines as times passes, which is why health experts recommend annual seasonal vaccinations, Healthline and the CDC noted. content: WELCOME, My Times LOGOUT SIGN IN Tue ,Sep 29, 2026Mumbai Mirror|Pune Mirror Home Bangalore Cover Story Crime Civic Other Elections Entertainment Bollywood Hollywood Reviews Lounge South Masala Videos sectionhomelist News Sports Entertainment Photos Entertainment News Sports Sports Cricket Football Tennis Others News State India World Business Opinion Ask the Sexpert Sunday Read You Code 560 Others Views Food Teen Spirit Blogs Loksabha Elections Photos Videos Schedule Campaign Tracker Modi Meter Coronavirus All Coronavirus Cover Story Crime Civic Other Elections News Photos Videos Bangalore Cover story Crime Civic Others Entertainment Bollywood Hollywood Reviews Lounge South Masala Videos News Sports Entertainment Photos Entertainment News Sports Sports Cricket Football Tennis Others News State India World Business Opinion Ask the Sexpert Sunday Read You Code 560 Others Views Food Teen Spirit Blogs Others Letters to the Editor Sci-Tech Leisure Trending Today Lit.Mus 2014 Home / Bangalore / Other / BMHealth: H1N1 cases rise in Bengaluru; doctors urge caution, not panic BMHealth: H1N1 cases rise in Bengaluru; doctors urge caution, not panic Updated: Sep 28, 2026, 21:08 IST Facebook Twitter Linkedin Email Share Facebook Twitter Linkedin Email Print this article Reduce font size Increase font size . Bengaluru is witnessing a seasonal rise in flu-like illnesses this monsoon, with H1N1 infections also being detected in increasing numbers. Private hospitals, clinics and diagnostic centres in the city say more patients are testing positive compared to last year. However, doctors and health officials stress that the situation is not alarming, with severe infections and hospitalisations remaining low. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has clarified that the virus currently circulating is the seasonal influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 strain and not a newly mutated or unusually dangerous variant. H1N1 usually begins with a sudden fever accompanied by body ache, sore throat, cough, headache and fatigue. Some patients may also develop vomiting or diarrhoea. While most infections respond to medication and rest, the illness can occasionally progress to breathing difficulty or pneumonia, particularly among vulnerable groups. Doctors advise people not to ignore a fever that persists beyond 24 to 48 hours and to avoid taking antibiotics without medical advice. Dr K Krishnamurthy from KK Clinic said, “The changing weather, high humidity, rainfall, crowded indoor spaces and poor ventilation are creating favourable conditions for respiratory infections to spread.” Doctors say H1N1 typically sees a rise during the monsoon and winter months, and this year’s increase is broadly following the usual seasonal pattern. Improved testing is also resulting in more confirmed cases. In some families, multiple members are developing flu-like symptoms, while many patients continue to experience fever, cough and body ache for five days or longer. Dr Sridhar Srinivasan, Consultant in Internal Medicine at Vasavi Hospitals said, “There has been a rise in H1N1 cases over the last month. The need for awareness currently with regard to wearing masks and maintaining hand hygiene is very much essential, as daily caseloads have been increasing across India.” Doctors caution that not every case of fever, cold or cough necessarily indicates H1N1. Dengue, chikungunya, malaria, the common cold and secondary bacterial infections can cause overlapping symptoms. Clinical assessment and, where required, testing help distinguish these illnesses. Doctors say caution without unnecessary fear remains the best approach. Maintaining respiratory hygiene, limiting exposure when symptomatic and seeking timely medical advice can help prevent complications as seasonal flu activity picks up across the city. H1N1: What to watch for Sudden high fever Persistent cough Sore throat Body ache and headache Extreme tiredness Vomiting or diarrhoea Breathlessness in severe cases Who needs extra caution? Senior citizens Young children Pregnant women People with diabetes Those with asthma, COPD or chronic heart or lung disease People with weakened immune systems Keep the flu at bay Stay home while feverish or unwell Wear a mask when symptomatic Wash hands frequently Improve indoor ventilation Avoid close contact and crowded places Stay hydrated and get adequate rest Take medicines only as prescribed Consider annual influenza vaccination, especially if you are at higher risk. Flu season is late and cases are up TD The New Daily Sep 23, 2026, updated Sep 23, 2026 Australia's flu cases were up in early September, at a time when they're usually falling. The weather is warming up and the hay fever season has begun, but more people are experiencing cases of influenza than expected for spring. In the two weeks to September 6, flu cases were up 27 per cent on the previous two weeks. And case numbers are rising. Video Player 12 00:00 00:00 Use Up/Down Arrow keys to increase or decrease volume. How is this year’s flu season different? This year, surveillance systems based in laboratories, data from members of the community, GPs and hospitals all suggest influenza activity has been lower than in previous years for most of the year. But influenza case numbers have increased since mid-August. So far, the majority of influenza cases have been due to the H3N2 subtype of influenza A, although some H1N1 and influenza B have also been reported. The H3N2 subtype has mostly been due to the “super K” strain that was associated with a late surge of cases in 2025. This strain seemed to be more transmissible than usual, although it didn’t cause more severe disease. There are also some differences in activity in different parts of Australia. NSW and Western Australia both had an increase in influenza activity from late June that was not seen in other other states and territories. You might like In Depth Is it safe to charge your phone overnight? In Depth When rogue AI agent ‘scaled a fence’, it reinforced the PM’s case What is the usual pattern of influenza in Australia? Since the Covid pandemic, influenza epidemiology has been more unpredictable than usual. Before the pandemic, influenza cases usually started to rise in June-July and peaked in August, falling to lower levels by late October. During the pandemic, influenza activity was essentially absent for 2020 and 2021, but resumed with the re-opening of international borders and relaxation of public health measures in 2022. You might like In Depth Is it safe to charge your phone overnight? In Depth When rogue AI agent ‘scaled a fence’, it reinforced the PM’s case The influenza seasons in 2022 and 2023 were unusually early, peaking in late June. Last year was also unusual, with an initial peak in mid-July and then persisting activity until late December. This was attributed to the “super K” strain of H3N2 influenza that has also been circulating this year. Influenza activity does vary between different parts of Australia. Tropical regions tend to get two peaks of influenza each year: One early in the year and a second around the same time as the other states. Why does flu season vary from year to year? The drivers of influenza transmission are still unknown, which makes long-term predictions difficult. In general, infectious diseases are an interaction between the “agent” (characteristics of the influenza virus) the “host” (characteristics of the people who are susceptible to influenza) and the environment that brings them together. The influenza virus changes from year to year, and each strain may have different properties, such as being able spread more readily, or to cause more severe disease. Apart from pandemics due to completely new strains, seasonal influenza is usually a small variation on the previously circulating strain. So most people have some degree of at least partial immunity to influenza, which may also be enhanced by vaccination. People’s behaviour can also impact influenza transmission. An obvious example is school holidays reducing transmission in school-aged children. Stay informed, daily The role of the environment is less clear with influenza, but it is likely some combinations of temperature and humidity may increase the spread. What else can cause flu-like illnesses? Influenza is not the only virus that causes flu-like symptoms. Other viruses such as rhinovirus can cause flu-like symptoms, but less commonly cause serious illness. However, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – and since 2020 SARS-CoV-2, the cause of Covid – can also cause significant illness. The pattern of RSV has been similar to previous years, and Covid activity continues to decline. What about influenza vaccines? Influenza vaccines are partially protective against influenza, and the degree of protection can vary year to year. Preliminary data this year suggests the influenza vaccine reduces the risk of hospitalisation with severe influenza by about 35 per cent. This is on the lower side when compared to estimates in previous years. The proportion of people who get a vaccine varies by age group. In older people (65 and over), around 60 per cent of people have received an influenza vaccine this year, down from around 70 per cent in 2022. In pre-school children (aged two-five years), 28 per cent have received a flu vaccine, similar to the figures reported in 2022. What does the unusual influenza season mean for me? The unusual pattern of influenza means it’s still worth getting an influenza vaccine now, if you haven’t had one earlier this year. Although there is some evidence that the protection from influenza vaccine does wane over three to six months, people vaccinated early in the season still have some protection. A second vaccine in the same season is generally not recommended. (The exceptions to this are young children who have not previously received an influenza vaccine, and people with specific conditions such as those receiving bone marrow transplants.) The influenza vaccine is free for high-risk groups including older people, young children and people with chronic medical illnesses. Talk to your pharmacist, GP, nurse or Aboriginal health practitioner. Influenza vaccines may also be available through workplace immunisation programs. Ask complex medical questions and find the latest clinical guidance for drugs & conditions with Medscape AI× EN RegisterLog In AI Mode Medscape News Canada Vaccine Advisory Group Offers Advice on Flu Vaccine Timing Shawn Radcliffe, MS DISCLOSURES DISCLOSURES Author Shawn Radcliffe, MS Health and Science Journalist Author Shawn Radcliffe, MS Health and Science Journalist September 24, 2026 27 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points The National Advisory Committee on Immunization (NACI), which makes recommendations for the use of vaccines for patients in Canada, released an updated statement for the 2026-2027 influenza season. NACI reaffirmed its guidance that the influenza vaccine be offered annually to anyone aged 6 months or older, except to those who cannot receive the vaccine because of medical reasons such as an allergy to a vaccine ingredient. The key changes in the recommendations include the inclusion of new evidence on the optimal timing of seasonal influenza vaccination. This section considers the seasonality of flu activity across Canada and the intraseasonal waning of influenza vaccine-induced immunity. The current evidence is “insufficient” to establish optimal timing for specific populations, so vaccination in early fall remains the best way to provide “sustained protection” throughout the season, according to the statement. The statement also includes updated guidance on seasonal influenza vaccination in the context of avian influenza. SUGGESTED FOR YOU “Although seasonal influenza vaccines do not protect against avian influenza A (H5N1) viruses, they may mitigate the severity of seasonal influenza and reduce the risk of coinfection with seasonal and avian influenza strains,” according to the statement. As a result, influenza vaccination is “particularly important” for individuals who are at higher risk for exposure to avian flu viruses. Waning Immunity and Optimal Timing The peak of the flu season is unpredictable, so the best time to receive the flu vaccine remains early fall, shortly after the vaccines are available, Matthew S. Miller, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biomedical sciences at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, told Medscape News Canada. “Failing to get vaccinated early creates increased risk of becoming infected before vaccination or before protective immune responses can be generated,” he said, pointing out that it takes a couple of weeks after vaccination for the immune system to generate protective immunity. For vulnerable individuals, “as soon as you can” is the best approach to vaccination, Brian Ward, MD, professor of medicine at McGill University in Montreal, agreed. Patients with a low risk for flu complications, however, can choose to wait until the flu is “in the news,” but this is an individual choice. Each flu season is different, which makes it challenging to shift recommendations ahead of time, Ward emphasized. For example, “some [seasons] start early, and some drag on,” he said, while “some are dominated by A strains early in the season, and B strains often come later.” Overall, “while we recognize that immunity from influenza vaccination wanes, it still offers protection for 6 months or more and therefore provides protection for most of the respiratory season,” said Jia Hu, MD, interim medical director of Immunization Programs and Vaccine Preventable Diseases Service at the BC Centre for Disease Control in Vancouver. “As a result, neither NACI nor other immunization advisory organizations recommend different approaches — such as a midseason booster — when it comes to influenza vaccination,” he added. Randomized controlled trials could provide additional evidence on changing the timing of immunization or the number of doses, said Miller. But “it would be challenging logistically and from a resources perspective to require more than one dose during a single season,” he said. Coordinating Multiple Vaccinations “We generally don’t recommend different timing for different groups of people,” said Hu. “However, it is not feasible to immunize an entire population all at once. So, in British Columbia, we offer the vaccine earlier for some groups at particularly high risk of severe influenza, such as those living in long-term care homes.” The recommendation for adults remains a single dose in early fall, Ward emphasized. “The efficacy of a second dose of the same vaccine in a prolonged flu season has never been well studied,” he said, “so [a second dose] isn’t recommended...even if [flu] cases are still actively happening very late in the season.” But “the one exception to this is young children [6 months to less than 9 years of age], who are recommended to receive two doses the first time they receive a seasonal influenza vaccine. But that has been a longstanding recommendation,” Miller pointed out. Influenza and COVID vaccines are updated and offered annually. The respiratory syncytial virus vaccine provides protection in older adults for at least 2 years, and it is not known whether additional doses are helpful. “These vaccines can be given together along with the flu shot if they are indicated for someone (or at any time before or after the flu shot),” said Ward. This approach is also helpful from a “programmatic perspective and for patient convenience,” Hu pointed out. But given that “seasonal waves of COVID remain somewhat unpredictable and misaligned with peak influenza season, it raises questions about whether coordinating timing of influenza and COVID vaccines is [always] practical,” said Miller. Miller, Ward, and Hu reported no relevant financial relationships. content: News Sports Autos Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH How long does flu shot last? What experts say this fall Jenna Prestininzi USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Sept. 25, 2026, 9:51 a.m. ET Hear this story The arrival of fall in Michigan means the peak of flu season is not far away, and experts say getting vaccinated now will give you protection throughout the season. The flu shot provides lifesaving protection against severe illness and prevents spreading the flu to your loved ones, according to the American Lung Association. Experts recommend getting your flu shot by late October, and even in September if possible, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Once you're vaccinated, it'll take about two weeks for antibodies offering protection against the illness to develop in your body, the CDC says. The vaccination will protect you throughout flu season. Immunity declines as times passes, which is why health experts recommend annual seasonal vaccinations, Healthline and the CDC noted. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has recommended updated flu vaccines to protect against the influenza A (H3N2) subclade K virus of the flu that spread during last year's flu season, the CDC said. Flu season in the U.S. typically is worst from October to May, peaking in the winter between December and February, the CDC and Cleveland Clinic said. You can get vaccinated at a local pharmacy or other health institutions across Michigan. Here's what to know before getting vaccinated. How long does the flu shot last? Once you're vaccinated against influenza (the flu), the flu shot takes around two weeks to develop antibodies in your body, offering protection against the illness, the CDC says. A vaccination is designed to protect you throughout the current flu season, and your body's immunity to the flu will decline as time goes on, Healthline said. The CDC recommends getting your seasonal flu vaccine each year to best protect yourself from the flu. When does flu season start? Flu season begins in the fall, typically in October, the Cleveland Clinic says. Flu season tends to peak in the winter months, between December and February, the CDC explained. What is the flu? The flu is a common respiratory illness you get from the influenza virus, the Cleveland Clinic said. What's new with flu vaccines? For the upcoming flu season, the Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration at a March 12 meeting recommended three egg-based vaccines and three cell or recombinant vaccines, the CDC said. This year's flu shot is a trivalent vaccine targeting three variations of the virus: two influenza A-type viruses that cover H1N1 and H3N2 strains, as well as an influenza B/Victoria lineage-type virus, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The new vaccines are designed to protect against the influenza A (H3N2) subclade K virus of the flu that spread during last year's flu season, the CDC said. The FDA shared the guidance with the manufacturers of FDA-approved seasonal flu vaccines, the CDC said. A new mRNA version of the seasonal flu shot called mFLUSIVA has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for use in people ages 50 and older. Where can you get the flu shot? Check with your local pharmacy, doctor's office or health department to set up your flu shot. Many health care providers offer walk-ins and appointments. How long does flu season last? Flu season lasts into the spring, usually slowing in May, the Cleveland Clinic says, but influenza viruses can spread year-round. Who should get the flu shot? The CDC recommends everyone 6 months and older get vaccinated against the flu. Those at higher risk for the flu include: Adults 65 and older Individuals with chronic health conditions Children 5 and younger Pregnant women How much does the flu shot cost? The flu shot may be free or low cost with most insurance options. The Detroit Free Press contributed. Contact Jenna Prestininzi: jprestininzi@freepress.com. Featured Weekly Ad

content: Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local Weather U.S. & World The Scene Politics Investigations Newsletters Cloudy 68o Watch 24/7 Trending 🗳️ Early voting 🏈 Commanders 🌡️ Forecast 🔍 4 More Context 👂 All Ears Find Help 📨 NBC4 Newsletters 📺 Watch 24/7 Our News Standards Expand Health This seasonal habit promotes healthy aging and may reduce dementia risk in older people In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, a doctor reveals how one routine vaccine can protect the body and brain as we age. By Caroline Kee | TODAY • Published September 26, 2026 • Updated on September 26, 2026 at 3:06 pm Getty Images Unwell senior man sneezing and blowing nose with napkin while on a walk in nature during autumn. Aging is inevitable, but there’s increasing evidence that it may be possible to prevent, or at least delay, age-related diseases, including cardiovascular disease and Alzheimer’s. Although life expectancy has soared in the United States over the past century, many people are living longer in poorer health. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. WATCH HERE That’s why many aging experts are shifting the focus away from lifespan. Instead, the goal is to maximize our “healthspan,” aka the number of years spent living into older age in good health. And slowing down biological aging often boils down to simple, healthy choices and preventive healthcare. Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel, an oncologist and professor of medical ethics at the University of Pennsylvania, previously spoke to TODAY.com about evidence-based habits to promote longevity, including staying up to date on routine vaccinations. There’s one vaccine in particular that’s especially important for adults over the age of 50, says Emanuel. Longevity tip of the day: Stay up to date with your flu vaccine to promote healthy aging U.S. & World The day's top national and international news. Walmart Inc. 3 hours ago Walmart says it's not using personal information to set prices as it expands digital shelf labels Death penalty 4 hours ago Tennessee is set to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years If you’re an adult who wants to age healthier, get your annual flu shot, says Emanuel, who authored “Eat Your Ice Cream: Six Simple Rules for a Long and Healthy Life.” The seasonal influenza vaccine is the most effective way to protect against severe illness, complications and death from flu. In addition to these benefits, there’s growing evidence that the flu shot may protect against age-related neurodegenerative diseases. “Cognitive decline is a serious worry, so (getting the flu shot) is one thing you can and should do,” says Emanuel. Why it matters As we get older, our body’s natural immune defenses gradually weaken, making it harder to fight off infections. People over the age of 65 face a much higher risk of getting very sick, becoming hospitalized or dying from the flu. “Thousands of people die every year from influenza,” says Emanuel. There’s increasing evidence showing that routine adult vaccines like the flu shot are associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer’s in older adults, TODAY.com previously reported. “Especially for people over 50, vaccines may reduce your risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” says Emanuel. In a 2026 study published in Neurology, researchers found that the high-dose flu shot is associated with a 55% lower risk of Alzheimer’s in adults over 65 in the years following vaccination. In addition to the flu shot, three other routine adult vaccines may cut dementia risk, says Ezekiel. These include the shingles vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine, and the diptheria, pertussis tetanus vaccine (Tdap). So if you’re looking to protect your body and brain as you get older, staying up to date on these shots is crucial, Emanuel says. How to get started If you have questions about the flu shot or which vaccine is appropriate for you, talk to your doctor. The 2026-2027 seasonal influenza vaccines are available and being rolled out at pharmacies, doctors’ offices, hospitals and clinics nationwide. There are multiple options available, including egg-based standard dose flu shots, high-dose flu shots and cell-based shots. For the first time, there is also an mRNA flu shot available to those 50 and older this year (though the dementia reduction findings only apply to the other types of flu vaccines.) They protect against three flu viruses (two influenza A and one influenza B strain), which are expected to circulate this winter. The best time to get a flu vaccine is in late September or October, before flu activity peaks. It takes about two weeks for the flu shot to take full effect, and this protection generally lasts about six months through the end of flu season.
